metaTitle: Water Bugs vs Cockroaches: Tell Them Apart
metaDescription: A true water bug is a pond insect that bites; the waterbug in your basement is usually an Oriental cockroach. See how to tell them apart.
h1: Water Bugs vs Cockroaches: How to Tell Which One You Found
dek: Why two unrelated insects share one nickname, how to tell a giant water bug from an Oriental or American cockroach by sight, and what each one means for your home.
excerpt: Two unrelated insects share the name water bug. Here is how to tell a biting giant water bug from an Oriental or American cockroach, and what to do about each.

quickAnswer.lead: **A true water bug is a pond insect that bites, while the waterbug in a basement or drain is usually an Oriental cockroach.** The giant water bug is brown, flat and up to about 2.5 inches long, with grasping front legs. [Penn State Extension](https://extension.psu.edu/oriental-cockroaches) says Oriental cockroaches earn the nickname from the dark, damp places they hide.
bullets: Giant water bugs are about 2 to 2.5 inches long, live in ponds, lakes and slow streams, and fly to lights on summer nights.
Oriental cockroaches are about 1 to 1.25 inches long, dark brown to nearly black, and do not fly.
American cockroaches are about 2 inches long, reddish brown, and the adults can fly on warm, humid evenings.
Mississippi State Extension describes a giant water bug bite as extremely painful but short-lived, with no long-term adverse effects.
Oriental cockroaches die within two weeks without water, so leaks and damp spots are the weak point.
Giant water bugs are not household pests, while Oriental and American cockroaches are.

body.text: Are water bugs and cockroaches the same insect?

No. Water bug is a nickname that has landed on two unrelated insects: the giant water bug, which lives in ponds and bites, and the Oriental cockroach, which hides in damp basements and drains. [Penn State Extension](https://extension.psu.edu/oriental-cockroaches) says Oriental cockroaches are often called water bugs because they favor dark, damp, cool places such as under sinks and washing machines, and the [University of California's cockroach guide](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/cockroaches/) notes that the same species is sometimes called a water bug or a black beetle.

The name fits the giant water bug better. [Missouri's Department of Conservation](https://www.mdc.mo.gov/discover-nature/field-guide/giant-water-bugs) describes a brownish, flattened, beetle-like insect that lives in ponds and sluggish water and eats insects, crayfish, frogs, fish and young turtles and snakes. The [University of Kentucky](https://www.uky.edu/Ag/CritterFiles/casefile/insects/bugs/giantwater/giantwater.htm) records the confusion running the other way, listing water roach among the giant water bug's other names.

The two call for opposite responses. A giant water bug is a pond animal that strayed toward a light and is best left alone, while a roach in the house is a pest that needs a plan. If you want the background on the species behind the nickname first, [the complete cockroach guide for US homes](/learn/cockroaches) covers all of them.
How can you tell a giant water bug from a cockroach?

Start with the front legs and the head. The [University of Kentucky](https://www.uky.edu/Ag/CritterFiles/casefile/insects/bugs/giantwater/giantwater.htm) describes giant water bugs with large, prey-grasping front legs and a sharp piercing beak, and Missouri adds long, oar-like hind legs built for swimming. [UC IPM](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/home-and-landscape/cockroaches/) describes cockroaches as broad, flattened insects with long antennae and a shield-shaped plate behind the head. Grasping front legs mean a water bug; long antennae and that shield-shaped plate mean a cockroach.

body.text: Behavior is a second clue. UC IPM describes cockroaches as mostly nocturnal insects that crawl quickly and may climb rough surfaces, and Penn State calls the Oriental cockroach sluggish, found at or below ground level and rarely on walls or upper floors. A large insect beside a lit doorway or floating in a swimming pool is more likely to be the aquatic one, as the next section explains.

If your insect matches neither column, compare it with [the beetles, crickets and wood roaches most often mistaken for a pest cockroach](/blog/bugs-that-look-like-cockroaches). A far smaller roach is probably another species, such as the one in [the German cockroach guide](/blog/german-cockroaches), and a small wingless insect may be a young roach, which [a photo guide to baby cockroaches by species](/blog/what-do-baby-cockroaches-look-like) helps you check.
What is a giant water bug, and why is one at my door?

A giant water bug is a large aquatic predator that sometimes leaves the water on summer nights and flies toward bright lights. [Mississippi State University Extension](https://extension.msstate.edu/newsletters/bugs-eye-view/2024/giant-water-bug-vol-10-no-08) says adults reach up to 2.5 inches, live in ponds, lakes and streams throughout the country, and are relatively common but rarely seen. On summer nights they sometimes crawl out of the water and fly, it adds, and they are attracted to artificial lights, sometimes crash-landing nearby. Missouri says these night flights occasionally end with a bug in a swimming pool.

In the water, it is an ambush hunter. Mississippi State reports that young nymphs eat other insects and small aquatic invertebrates, while large nymphs and adults take minnows, tadpoles, frogs, and small snakes and turtles. The bug grabs prey with its front legs and injects saliva that paralyzes the victim and begins digesting it. Missouri calls giant water bugs generally beneficial because they consume mosquito larvae.

One oddity helps with identification. Missouri reports that the female lays her eggs in a flat cluster on the male's back, and that an egg-laden male cannot fly or mate until the eggs hatch. Kentucky adds that only some species do this. A water bug carrying a mat of eggs is therefore a male that is not about to fly to your porch light.

body.text: Which cockroaches do people call water bugs?

Mostly the Oriental cockroach, a dark, slow insect of damp, low places that does not fly. UC IPM lists it at about 1.25 inches and almost black, living in cool, dark, damp places such as garages, basements, water meter boxes and drains, and unable to climb smooth vertical surfaces. Penn State puts adults at about an inch, very dark brown to nearly black with a greasy sheen. The two sources differ by a fraction of an inch, so expect something between 1 and 1.25 inches.

Males have short wings that cover about three-quarters of the abdomen, and females have only small, functionless wing pads, and UC IPM says the species does not fly. Penn State places the species indoors under porches, in drains, sewers, crawl spaces and damp basements, and gathered around leaks. Outdoors it lives in leaf litter, bark mulch around foundations, water valve pits and garbage areas, and it may move inside during dry spells to find humidity.
What about the American cockroach?

The American cockroach is the larger, reddish brown species that shares the Oriental cockroach's damp territory. UC IPM lists it at about 2 inches with light-colored edges on the plate behind the head, and says adults can fly, especially on warm, humid evenings. It prefers warm, humid conditions, usually above 82°F (28°C), in places such as sewers, water meter boxes, storm drains and steam tunnels, and UC IPM says it readily lives outdoors under the right conditions. That overlap in size and in warm-evening flights is why a large flying insect at night can be either one. Which cockroaches really fly, and how well, is laid out in [the species-by-species guide to flying roaches](/blog/can-cockroaches-fly).
The [palmetto bug guide](/blog/palmetto-bugs) compares the American cockroach with the other large roaches that go by that name, with photos.
Do water bugs bite?

Giant water bugs do, and the bite hurts; cockroach bites are a separate and much smaller question. Missouri says a giant water bug that is handled or disturbed by waders delivers an extremely painful bite, which is where the nickname toe-biter comes from. Mississippi State also calls the bites extremely painful, but says the pain is relatively short-lived with no long-term adverse effects, and that bites are rare because people seldom meet the insects. The University of Kentucky says bites can be painful and that some people have medically serious reactions, though it calls this very rare.

For most people, then, the sources describe sharp but short-lived pain, and Kentucky's note means a serious reaction is very rare but not impossible. Contact a healthcare provider if pain or swelling keeps getting worse, if symptoms spread, or if you have ever reacted badly to an insect bite. For the cockroaches, [what is actually documented about cockroach bites](/blog/do-cockroaches-bite) separates rare bites from the more common health issues covered next.
Are water bugs or cockroaches dangerous?

A giant water bug is a painful nuisance, and the cockroaches carry the larger health risk. The [EPA](https://www.epa.gov/asthma/asthma-triggers-gain-control) says certain proteins in cockroach feces and saliva can cause allergic reactions or trigger asthma symptoms in some people, and that droppings or body parts of cockroaches can trigger asthma.

Penn State links Oriental cockroaches to gastroenteritis, dysentery and diarrhea through disease organisms carried on their legs and bodies. It also lists allergic reactions to their droppings and shed skins, including sneezing, watery eyes, nasal congestion and asthma. UC IPM says the American cockroach is capable of transmitting the bacteria *Salmonella* and *Shigella*, which cause food poisoning. The sources use cautious wording such as capable of and linked to, so read these as documented risks, not as a certainty that any one roach has made someone sick.

If anyone in the home has asthma or allergy symptoms that are worse indoors and you are finding cockroaches, tell their healthcare provider about the infestation. The giant water bug has no comparable household risk; Kentucky says giant water bugs are not considered pests.
What should you do about a giant water bug?

Leave it alone, or move it outside without touching it, because it is not a household pest and the bite is the only real risk. Missouri describes the painful bite coming when waders handle or disturb the insect, and Mississippi State says bites are rare because encounters are infrequent. A bug stranded on a porch can be nudged into a container with a piece of cardboard and released near water, and one in a pool can be lifted out with a net.

Because adults are drawn to artificial lights, a bright light near a pond or pool is the likely draw. The sources describe that attraction, but none tests a lighting change as a fix, so there is no evidence-based method to offer. What they do show is that the visits are seasonal: Mississippi State ties the flights to summer nights.
How do you get rid of the cockroaches called water bugs?

Cut off water, close the gaps, and put bait where the roaches live. That is the pattern in the extension guidance, and it targets what these species need most: Penn State reports that Oriental cockroaches die within two weeks without water, although they can live a month without food when water is available.

items: **Dry out and clean up.** Penn State calls removing food, moisture and the harborages roaches shelter in the first step in treatment. The EPA's asthma guidance adds keeping counters, sinks, tables and floors clean and free of clutter, cleaning dishes, crumbs and spills right away, and storing food in airtight containers.

**Seal the entry routes.** UC IPM recommends sealing cracks and other openings and fitting door sweeps and weather stripping on doors and windows. It notes that American cockroaches foraging from sewers reach ground floors especially where pipes are damaged, screens are missing or drain water traps are faulty, so those are worth checking too. Penn State adds caulking in closets and cabinets and under the sink, and [how cockroaches get into a home and how to close each route](/blog/where-do-cockroaches-come-from) walks through the rest.

**Monitor with sticky traps.** Penn State suggests setting sticky traps against walls and in corners at several sites for a week to learn how widespread the problem is. A guide to [how glue traps and bait stations do different jobs](/blog/best-roach-traps-canada) explains what traps can and cannot do.

**Bait the places they live.** For outdoor-living roaches, UC IPM recommends placing baits in water meter boxes, drains or under concrete slabs. Penn State lists bait active ingredients such as hydramethylnon, fipronil, boric acid and abamectin, placed where roaches harbor, and [why bait beats spray for cockroaches](/blog/best-cockroach-killer-canada) explains the reasoning.

body.title: Read the label first
body.text: Baits, dusts and sprays are pesticides. Use a product only where and how its label directs, and keep it away from children, pets and food. The EPA cautions that insecticides can harm people as well as pests and recommends choosing lower-risk methods.

Expect it to take time. UC IPM reports that Oriental cockroaches need 1 to 2 years or more to develop from nymph to adult, and that a female and her offspring can produce nearly 200 cockroaches in a year, so the population builds slowly but steadily while the damp conditions remain. A longer bait-first sequence is in [a step-by-step cockroach removal plan](/blog/how-to-get-rid-of-cockroaches-canada).
When should you call a professional?

Call one if you keep finding cockroaches after the moisture is fixed and bait is down, if they seem to come from shared walls or sewer lines in a multi-unit building, or if someone in the home has asthma and the infestation is established. In an apartment, report the problem to the property manager as well.

A recurring problem at one drain may be a plumbing fault. UC IPM links cockroach entry from sewers to damaged pipes and faulty drain water traps, and those are repairs for a plumber, not something a pesticide can fix. A giant water bug at your door, by contrast, needs no professional at all.

faqs.question: Can giant water bugs fly?
faqs.answer: Yes. Mississippi State Extension says giant water bugs sometimes crawl out of the water on summer nights and fly, and that they are drawn to artificial lights. Missouri's Department of Conservation says these night flights occasionally land them in swimming pools. Among the cockroaches, UC IPM reports that American cockroach adults can fly, especially on warm, humid evenings, while Oriental cockroaches do not fly. A large insect circling a light at night could therefore be either a giant water bug or an American cockroach, and the legs, size and color sort them out.

faqs.question: Is a giant water bug bite dangerous?
faqs.answer: Mississippi State Extension calls the bite extremely painful but says the pain is relatively short-lived and that there are no long-term adverse effects. The University of Kentucky says bites can be painful and that some people have medically serious reactions, though it calls this very rare. Contact a healthcare provider if the pain or swelling keeps getting worse, if symptoms spread, or if you have ever had an allergic reaction to an insect bite.

faqs.question: Why do I keep finding Oriental cockroaches in my basement?
faqs.answer: Oriental cockroaches seek cool, damp, dark places, and a basement with leaks, a floor drain or a crawl space offers all three. Penn State Extension says they enter in food packages and laundry and under doors, and may move indoors during dry spells to find humidity. Without water they die within two weeks, so repairing leaks and drying damp areas is the most useful step. Sealing cracks and placing bait where they live completes the job.

faqs.question: Can water bugs come up through drains?
faqs.answer: The cockroaches called water bugs can. UC IPM says Oriental cockroaches live in drains and water meter boxes, and that American cockroaches in sewers occasionally forage into ground-floor buildings, especially when pipes are damaged, screens are missing or drain water traps are faulty. The sources describe giant water bugs as living in ponds, slow streams and wetlands, not in plumbing. Sealing cracks and other openings is part of UC IPM's advice, and its mention of damaged pipes and faulty traps points to plumbing repairs as well.

faqs.question: Do giant water bugs eat mosquitoes?
faqs.answer: They eat the larvae. Missouri's Department of Conservation calls giant water bugs generally beneficial because they consume mosquito larvae. Larvae are only part of the diet, though: large nymphs and adults also eat minnows, tadpoles, frogs and small snakes and turtles, according to Mississippi State Extension. None of the sources reviewed here claims that the giant water bugs in a pond prevent a mosquito problem, so treat them as one natural predator among many and not as a control method.
